newsitem.title: UK: Millions in UK may face C5 reception problems.
newsitem.headline: Millions in UK may face C5 reception problems.

text.p: Millions of Britons may need new aerials to pick up a fifth terrestrial television channel when it begins broadcasting in March, the channel said on Friday.
Channel 5 spokeswoman Sally Osman said the station had acknowledged all along that there could be reception problems in some areas.

She said it would not be clear how many homes would be affected until more test transmissions are carried out ahead of the planned March 30 launch. But the channel estimates that three million households could be affected and the industry says the figure could be as high as four million.
Osman said Channel 5 would address the reception problem in a marketing campaign ahead of the launch.
"Our advice to consumers is not to spend any money on aerials for the moment," she said.

Channel 5 engineers are visiting millions of homes up and down the country to retune video recorders to avoid interference from the new channel's signal. That exercise is costing the channel 150 million stg.
But consumers will have to pay for new or improved aerials out of their own pockets.
Tim Jenks, technical executive of industry group, The Confederation of Aerial Industries, said the cost was likely to range between 40 and 150 stg per household.
"The broadcasting spectrum was initially meant for four channels. Some of the frequencies that Channel 5 will use are well away from the existing bandwidth," Jenks said.
This meant some viewers in areas like Humberside in eastern England could have clear reception for the four existing channels but a grainy Channel 5 with their existing aerials.
Channel 5 Broadcasting is a consortium comprising the UK's United News & Media Plc, Pearson Plc, Luxembourg broadcast group CLT and U.S investment firm Warburg Pincus.
